claim: The study profiled PBMCs from eight patients hospitalized for CAP caused by SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19), eight patients hospitalized for CAP caused by either Influenza A or other pathogens, and four non-infectious control subjects.
source: We profiled PBMCs from eight patients hospitalized for CAP caused by SARS-CoV-2 (henceforth referred to as COVID-19), eight patients hospitalized for CAP caused by either Influenza A or other pathogens (all sampled before the start of the COVID-19 pandemic), and four non-infectious control subjects visiting the outpatient clinic without signs of acute infection (Table 1 for summary data, Supplementary file 1 for individual patient data).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number and types of patients included in the study cohort.

claim: The groups were matched for age, sex, and disease severity using the Modified Early Warning Score.
source: We matched the groups for age, sex, and—the patients—for disease severity using the Modified Early Warning Score (Churpek et al., 2017; Subbe et al., 2001).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the matching criteria used for the study groups, with citations supporting the use of the Modified Early Warning Score.

claim: Samples from patients were obtained within 48 hr of admission to the general hospital ward.
source: Samples from patients were obtained within 48 hr of admission to the general hospital ward, none of the patients received systemic corticosteroid therapy prior to sampling.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the timing of sample collection relative to hospital admission.

claim: None of the patients received systemic corticosteroid therapy prior to sampling.
source: Samples from patients were obtained within 48 hr of admission to the general hospital ward, none of the patients received systemic corticosteroid therapy prior to sampling.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that no patients received systemic corticosteroids before sampling.

claim: Patients with COVID-19 reported a longer duration of symptoms prior to hospital admission.
source: Patients with COVID-19 reported a longer duration of symptoms prior to hospital admission.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this difference in symptom duration between groups.

claim: Lymphocyte counts were reduced in both patient groups but not significantly different.
source: Lymphocyte counts were reduced in both patient groups but not significantly different, whereas neutrophil counts were significantly higher in patients with non-COVID-19 CAP.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the lymphocyte count findings in both patient groups.

claim: Neutrophil counts were significantly higher in patients with non-COVID-19 CAP.
source: Lymphocyte counts were reduced in both patient groups but not significantly different, whereas neutrophil counts were significantly higher in patients with non-COVID-19 CAP.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that neutrophil counts were significantly higher in non-COVID-19 CAP patients.

claim: All patients classified as COVID-19 had a positive PCR for SARS-CoV-2.
source: All patients classified as COVID-19 had a positive PCR for SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the diagnostic criterion for COVID-19 classification.

claim: Three patients had a positive PCR for Influenza A.
source: In the patients without COVID-19, three had a positive PCR for Influenza A—one of whom also had a positive blood culture for Streptococcus pneumoniae—and one patient had a positive sputum culture for Haemophilus influenzae.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the microbiological findings in non-COVID-19 patients.

claim: One Influenza A patient also had a positive blood culture for Streptococcus pneumoniae.
source: In the patients without COVID-19, three had a positive PCR for Influenza A—one of whom also had a positive blood culture for Streptococcus pneumoniae—and one patient had a positive sputum culture for Haemophilus influenzae.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this co-infection case.

claim: One patient had a positive sputum culture for Haemophilus influenzae.
source: In the patients without COVID-19, three had a positive PCR for Influenza A—one of whom also had a positive blood culture for Streptococcus pneumoniae—and one patient had a positive sputum culture for Haemophilus influenzae.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this microbiological finding.

claim: None of the patients were admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) during their hospital stay.
source: None of the patients were admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) during their hospital stay, one patient with COVID-19 died in the hospital as a result of the disease.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that no patients required ICU admission.

claim: One patient with COVID-19 died in the hospital as a result of the disease.
source: None of the patients were admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) during their hospital stay, one patient with COVID-19 died in the hospital as a result of the disease.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports this mortality outcome.

claim: Post quality control, 16,192 cells from all profiled samples were analyzed.
source: Post quality control, we analyzed 16,192 cells from all profiled samples.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the total number of cells analyzed after quality control.

claim: UMAP dimensionality reduction of the transcriptome identified 13 clusters of myeloid and lymphoid immune cells in COVID-19 patients and non-infectious controls.
source: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) dimensionality reduction of the transcriptome of all individual cells from these subjects identified 13 clusters of myeloid and lymphoid immune cells (Figure 1b,c).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of clusters identified, and Figure 1b,c shows the UMAP visualization of these clusters.

claim: Patients with COVID-19 exhibited a decrease in monocytes and memory B cells compared with non-infectious control subjects.
source: When compared with age- and sex-matched non-infectious control subjects, patients with COVID-19 exhibited stark differences in the proportional composition of cell clusters, including a decrease in monocytes and memory B cells, and an increase in naive B cells (Figure 1c,d).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes these proportional differences, and Figure 1c,d shows the correlation plot depicting cluster enrichment.

claim: Patients with COVID-19 exhibited an increase in naive B cells compared with non-infectious control subjects.
source: When compared with age- and sex-matched non-infectious control subjects, patients with COVID-19 exhibited stark differences in the proportional composition of cell clusters, including a decrease in monocytes and memory B cells, and an increase in naive B cells (Figure 1c,d).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this proportional increase, and Figure 1c,d shows the correlation plot.

claim: Patients with COVID-19 showed a striking proportional increase in a specific T cell cluster and NK cells.
source: While some lymphocyte clusters were relatively decreased, we found a striking proportional increase in a specific T cell cluster and NK cells in patients with COVID-19.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this proportional increase in specific cell types.

claim: The expanded T cell cluster in COVID-19 mainly expressed low levels of surface CD27 and variable levels of CD45RA, resembling the terminally differentiated effector memory re-expressing CD45RA (EMRA) phenotype.
source: This expanded T cell cluster mainly expressed low levels of surface CD27 and variable levels of CD45RA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d), resembling the terminally differentiated effector memory re-expressing CD45RA (EMRA) phenotype as defined by classical flow cytometry (CCR7−CD27−CD45RA+; Martin and Badovinac, 2018).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the surface marker expression pattern and provides a citation for the EMRA phenotype definition. Figure 1—figure supplement 1d shows the CD27 and CD45RA expression.

claim: The CD8 EMRA-like T cell cluster was almost entirely composed of cells from patients with COVID-19.
source: In fact, these cells (that we will henceforth refer to as CD8 EMRA-like T cells) formed a cluster almost entirely composed of cells from patients with COVID-19 (Figure 1c and Figure 1—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the composition of this cluster, and the referenced figures show the distribution.

claim: CD8 EMRA-like T cells expressed low levels of IL7R (encoding for CD127) and CCR7 at the transcript level.
source: At the transcript level, the EMRA-like T cells expressed low levels of the canonical markers IL7R (encoding for CD127) and CCR7.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the transcript-level expression of these markers.

claim: CD8 EMRA-like T cells exhibited remarkably high expression of genes related to cytotoxicity and killing, such as GZMB, GZMH, PRF1, and NKG7.
source: The CD8 EMRA-like T cells exhibited remarkably high expression of genes related to cytotoxicity and killing—seemingly on par with NK cells—such as GZMB, GZMH, PRF1, and NKG7.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the high expression of these cytotoxicity-related genes.

claim: CD8 EMRA-like T cells were marked by high expression of ITGB1 (CD29), which has been described as a marker of T cells with increased cytotoxicity.
source: These cells were also marked by the high expression of ITGB1 (CD29), which has recently been described as a marker of T cells with increased cytotoxicity (Nicolet et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the high expression of ITGB1 and cites a reference supporting its association with cytotoxicity.

claim: The NK cell cluster was enriched in genes corresponding to type I and, to a lesser extent, type II interferon signaling pathways.
source: The NK cell cluster was enriched in genes corresponding to type I and, to a lesser extent, type II interferon signaling pathways (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b,c).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this enrichment, and the referenced figure shows the pathway analysis.

claim: NK cells from COVID-19 patients showed marked upregulation of pathways related to a type I interferon response and other antiviral responses compared to control subjects.
source: We then compared the expression levels of genes within the NK cell cluster between patients with COVID-19 and control subjects (Figure 1f) and discovered marked upregulation of pathways related to a type I interferon response and other antiviral responses in patients with COVID-19 (Biological Process Gene Ontology pathway analysis; Figure 1g).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this upregulation, and Figures 1f and 1g show the differential expression and pathway analysis.

claim: A broad pattern of type I interferon responses was observed across all cell clusters in COVID-19, statistically significant in several clusters including NK cells.
source: Transposing this NK cell cluster-derived type I interferon response signature to the other cell clusters revealed a broad pattern of type I interferon responses across all clusters, statistically significant in several clusters, including NK cells (two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test p<0.05; Figure 1h).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this broad pattern with statistical significance, and Figure 1h shows the enrichment scores across clusters.

claim: UMAP dimensionality reduction of CAP-flu, CAP-other, and control samples revealed 13 clusters of cells.
source: We next investigated the immune features of patients with CAP caused by Influenza A (CAP-flu) or other pathogens (CAP-other), as compared with matched non-infectious controls. UMAP dimensionality reduction revealed 13 clusters of cells (Figure 2a,c; and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–c for top DEGs and surface protein expression).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of clusters identified, and the referenced figures show the UMAP visualization.

claim: Patients with CAP-flu showed a proportional increase of CD8 EMRA-like T cell and NK cell clusters similar to COVID-19.
source: Akin to what we observed in patients with COVID-19, patients with CAP-flu showed a proportional increase of CD8 EMRA-like T cell and NK cell clusters (Figure 2b,c; cluster distribution per subject in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this similarity between CAP-flu and COVID-19, and the referenced figures show the proportional distributions.

claim: Patients with CAP-other had higher levels of the CD8 EM and naïve T cell clusters.
source: Patients with CAP-other had higher levels of the CD8 EM and naïve T cell clusters (Figure 2c).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this proportional difference, and Figure 2c shows the correlation plot.

claim: Both CAP-flu and CAP-other patients showed a decrease in memory B cells when compared with control subjects.
source: Both CAP-flu and CAP-other patients showed a decrease in memory B cells when compared with control subjects (Figure 2c).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this shared decrease, and Figure 2c shows the correlation plot.

claim: CD8 EMRA-like T cells were characterized by genes related to cytotoxicity and activation signals, such as GNLY, GZMB, TYROBP, and FGFBP.
source: CD8 EMRA-like T cells were characterized by genes related to cytotoxicity and activation signals, such as GNLY, GZMB, TYROBP, and FGFBP, which were also highly expressed by NK cells.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the gene expression characteristics of CD8 EMRA-like T cells.

claim: Among the top upregulated genes in the CD8 EM-cluster were GZMK and genes related to MHC class II (HLD-DRB1 and CD74).
source: To elucidate the transcriptional states of the differentially expanded T cell subsets between CAP-flu and CAP-other patients, we examined the top DEGs between CD8 EM T and CD8 EMRA-like cells (Figure 2d): among the top upregulated genes in the CD8 EM-cluster, we identified GZMK and genes related to MHC class II (HLD-DRB1 and CD74).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes these upregulated genes, and Figure 2d shows the heatmap of gene expression.

claim: Patients with CAP-flu exhibited a clear increase in classical monocytes when compared with patients with CAP-other and control subjects.
source: Patients with CAP-flu exhibited a clear increase in classical monocytes when compared with patients with CAP-other and control subjects (Figure 2b,c).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this proportional increase, and the referenced figures show the distribution.

claim: Patients with CAP-other demonstrated a clear increase in non-classical monocytes, contributing nearly all cells in this cluster.
source: Patients with CAP-other demonstrated a clear increase in non-classical monocytes, contributing nearly all cells in this cluster (Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this proportional increase, and the referenced figures show the distribution.

claim: Classical monocytes were mostly CD14+ and CD16−, whereas non-classical monocytes were CD14dim and CD16+.
source: In line with their transcriptome, classical monocytes were mostly CD14+ and CD16−, whereas non-classical monocytes were CD14dim and CD16+.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the surface marker expression patterns of these monocyte subsets.

claim: Classical monocytes from patients with CAP-flu displayed upregulation of genes involved in pro-inflammatory processes, such as EGR-1, FKB5, and AREG.
source: Classical monocytes from patients with CAP-flu displayed upregulation of a variety of genes involved in pro-inflammatory processes, such as EGR-1 (Pang et al., 2020), FKB5 (Zannas et al., 2019), and AREG (Zaiss et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the upregulation of these pro-inflammatory genes with supporting citations.

claim: Classical monocytes from CAP-flu patients transcribed several genes encoding for the S100 protein family, such as S100A4, S100A8, S100A9, and S100A12, which were recently implicated in COVID-19.
source: Classical monocytes also transcribed several genes encoding for the S100 protein family, such as S100A4, S100A8, S100A9, and S100A12, which were recently implicated in COVID-19 (Ren et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the expression of S100 family genes and cites a reference linking them to COVID-19.

claim: Classical monocytes from CAP-flu patients showed substantially reduced expression of genes related to MHC class II.
source: Strikingly, we observed a concurrent substantially reduced expression of genes related to MHC class II (Figure 2f), a quintessential feature of sepsis-induced immune suppression that has been associated with secondary infections and long-term mortality (Hotchkiss et al., 2013; Venet and Monneret, 2018).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this reduced expression with supporting citations, and Figure 2f shows the differential expression.

claim: Reduced HLA-DR expression on the cell surface of classical monocytes in patients with CAP-flu confirmed the transcriptional pattern at the protein level.
source: Reduced HLA-DR expression on the cell surface of classical monocytes in patients with CAP-flu confirmed this transcriptional pattern at the protein level (Figure 2i).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this protein-level confirmation, and Figure 2i shows the density plot of HLA-DR expression.

claim: UMAP dimensionality reduction of COVID-19, CAP-flu, and CAP-other samples revealed 15 clusters of myeloid and lymphoid cells.
source: Next, we directly compared COVID-19, CAP-flu, and CAP-other to delineate the shared and unique immune features between these disease groups. UMAP dimensionality reduction of all cells of these groups revealed 15 clusters of myeloid and lymphoid cells (the full UMAP of all identified clusters, the distribution per individual patient, and the DEGs and proteins between all clusters are depicted in Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of clusters identified, and the referenced figures show the UMAP visualization.

claim: Comparing the proportional composition of immune cells between diseases revealed a significant expansion of NK cells in COVID-19.
source: Comparing the proportional composition of immune cells between diseases revealed a significant expansion of NK cells in COVID-19, an expansion of monocytes in CAP-flu, and an overall expansion of T cells in CAP-other (Figure 3c).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this proportional expansion, and Figure 3c shows the correlation plot.

claim: Comparing the proportional composition of immune cells between diseases revealed an expansion of monocytes in CAP-flu.
source: Comparing the proportional composition of immune cells between diseases revealed a significant expansion of NK cells in COVID-19, an expansion of monocytes in CAP-flu, and an overall expansion of T cells in CAP-other (Figure 3c).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this proportional expansion, and Figure 3c shows the correlation plot.

claim: Comparing the proportional composition of immune cells between diseases revealed an overall expansion of T cells in CAP-other.
source: Comparing the proportional composition of immune cells between diseases revealed a significant expansion of NK cells in COVID-19, an expansion of monocytes in CAP-flu, and an overall expansion of T cells in CAP-other (Figure 3c).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this proportional expansion, and Figure 3c shows the correlation plot.

claim: Overall monocyte HLA-DR surface protein expression in COVID-19 was on par with CAP-flu, and lower than in CAP-other.
source: Overall monocyte HLA-DR surface protein expression in COVID-19 was on par with CAP-flu, and lower than in CAP-other.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the comparative HLA-DR expression levels across disease groups.

claim: Fewer cells were observed in the naive CD4/CD8 T cell cluster in COVID-19 and CAP-flu as compared with CAP-other.
source: We observed fewer cells in the naive CD4/CD8 T cell cluster in COVID-19 and CAP-flu as compared with CAP-other, whereas the CD8 EMRA-like 2 T cell cluster was clearly expanded in CAP-flu (Figure 4b; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1c for the correlation plot of all identified clusters).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this proportional difference, and the referenced figures show the distribution.

claim: The CD8 EMRA-like 2 T cell cluster was clearly expanded in CAP-flu.
source: We observed fewer cells in the naive CD4/CD8 T cell cluster in COVID-19 and CAP-flu as compared with CAP-other, whereas the CD8 EMRA-like 2 T cell cluster was clearly expanded in CAP-flu (Figure 4b; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1c for the correlation plot of all identified clusters).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this proportional expansion, and the referenced figures show the distribution.

claim: The CD8 EMRA-like 2 cluster expanded in CAP-flu showed increased expression of genes related to cytotoxicity, activation and inflammation—such as GZMB, GNLY, TYROBP, HOPX, and CCL5.
source: To infer functional differences in T cell subsets, we looked at the top DEGs between the two EMRA-like T cell clusters (Figure 4c). We noted increased expression of genes related to cytotoxicity, activation and inflammation—such as GZMB, GNLY, TYROBP, HOPX, and CCL5—in the CD8 EMRA-like two cluster that was expanded in CAP-flu.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this gene expression pattern, and Figure 4c shows the violin plots of gene expression.

claim: A higher proportion of granulysin+ NK cells was found in CAP-flu, whereas the other (granulysin negative) NK cell cluster was highest in COVID-19.
source: In line with high GNLY expression in the EMRA-like 2 T cell cluster expanded in CAP-flu, we found a higher proportion of granulysin+ NK cells in CAP-flu, whereas the other (granulysin negative) NK cell cluster was highest in COVID-19 (Figure 4b,c).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes these proportional differences, and the referenced figures show the distribution.

claim: The NK cell cluster expanded in COVID-19 expressed higher levels of the interferon-stimulated gene IFITM3 than the cluster expanded in CAP-flu.
source: Interestingly, the NK cell cluster expanded in COVID-19 expressed higher levels of the interferon-stimulated gene IFITM3 (Figure 4d) than the cluster expanded in CAP-flu.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this differential expression, and Figure 4d shows the violin plots.

claim: Gene Ontology enrichment of the genes upregulated in granulysin+ NK cells from patients with COVID-19 exposed a clear type I interferon response.
source: Gene Ontology enrichment of the genes upregulated in granulysin+ NK cells from patients with COVID-19 exposed a clear type I interferon response (Figure 4f).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this pathway enrichment, and Figure 4f shows the bar plot of pathway analysis.

claim: A pronounced type I interferon signature was found among virtually all T and NK cell clusters in patients with COVID-19, particularly in the EMRA-like T cell clusters and both NK cell clusters.
source: When comparing this pathway between disease groups in all T and NK cell clusters, we found this pronounced type I interferon signature among virtually all clusters in patients with COVID-19, particularly in the EMRA-like T cell clusters and both NK cell clusters (Figure 4g,h, statistically significant in the CD8 EMRA-like 2 and granulysin+ NK cell clusters, two-sided Kruskal-Wallis test with post hoc Dunn's test BH-adjusted p<0.05).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this signature with statistical significance, and Figures 4g and 4h show the heatmap and boxplots.

claim: Classical monocytes were proportionally expanded in both CAP groups, albeit primarily in patients with CAP-flu.
source: Classical monocytes were proportionally expanded in both CAP groups, albeit primarily in patients with CAP-flu (Figure 5b).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this proportional expansion, and Figure 5b shows the correlation plot.

claim: The intermediate monocyte cluster was prominently expanded in patients with COVID-19.
source: The intermediate monocyte cluster was prominently expanded in patients with COVID-19, whereas the non-classical monocyte cluster showed a clear expansion in the CAP-other patients.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this proportional expansion.

claim: The non-classical monocyte cluster showed a clear expansion in the CAP-other patients.
source: The intermediate monocyte cluster was prominently expanded in patients with COVID-19, whereas the non-classical monocyte cluster showed a clear expansion in the CAP-other patients.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this proportional expansion.

claim: In classical monocytes (proportionally higher in patients with CAP-flu) the majority of upregulated genes was related to ribosomes and viral transcription.
source: In classical monocytes (proportionally higher in patients with CAP-flu) the majority of upregulated genes was related to ribosomes and viral transcription (Figure 5c,d).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this gene expression pattern, and Figures 5c and 5d show the heatmap and pathway analysis.

claim: The intermediate monocytes (consistently present in COVID-19) were characterized by a pronounced antiviral, interferon-driven response, as illustrated by the upregulation of interferon-inducible and stimulated genes (IFI6, IFI27, IFI44L, and ISG15, SIGLEC1).
source: The intermediate monocytes (consistently present in COVID-19) were characterized by a pronounced antiviral, interferon-driven response, as illustrated by the upregulation of both interferon-inducible and stimulated genes (IFI6, IFI27, IFI44L, and ISG15, SIGLEC1; Figure 5c,e).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this gene expression pattern, and Figures 5c and 5e show the heatmap and pathway analysis.

claim: The high expression of APOBEC3A and MX1 in intermediate monocytes underlined increased antiviral potential.
source: The high expression of APOBEC3A and MX1, involved in restricting viral activity in monocytes through RNA editing (Sharma et al., 2015; Verhelst et al., 2012), underlined this increased antiviral potential.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the expression of these genes and cites references supporting their antiviral function.

claim: The upregulated DEGs of the non-classical monocyte cluster (predominantly present in CAP-other) included genes involved in MHC class II antigen-presenting, Fc receptors (FCGR3A and FCER1G), the complement system (C1QA and CFD), and multiple genes associated with cell activation (AIF1, LST1, and SMIM25).
source: The upregulated DEGs of the non-classical monocyte cluster (predominantly present in CAP-other) were more heterogeneous: they expressed genes involved in MHC class II antigen-presenting, Fc receptors (FCGR3A and FCER1G), the complement system (C1QA and CFD), and multiple genes associated with cell activation (AIF1, LST1, and SMIM25; Figure 5c,f).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this gene expression pattern, and Figures 5c and 5f show the heatmap and pathway analysis.

claim: CD8 EMRA T cells effectively kill virus-infected cells, have a varying proliferation capacity, and represent the predominant phenotype in circulating CD8 T cells specific for respiratory viruses in adults.
source: CD8 EMRA T cells effectively kill virus-infected cells, have a varying proliferation capacity, and (together with CD8 EM T cells) represent the predominant phenotype in circulating CD8 T cells specific for respiratory viruses in adults (Martin and Badovinac, 2018; Schmidt and Varga, 2018; Verma et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes these characteristics of CD8 EMRA T cells with supporting citations.

claim: Other studies in COVID-19 similarly reported CD8 T cells that were highly activated, had increased cytotoxic potential, and exhibited characteristics of EMRA (or sometimes EM) cells.
source: Other studies in COVID-19 similarly reported CD8 T cells that were highly activated (De Biasi et al., 2020; Kuri-Cervantes et al., 2020b; Mathew et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020) had increased cytotoxic potential (Kuri-Cervantes et al., 2020b; Zhang et al., 2020) and exhibited characteristics of EMRA (or sometimes EM) cells (De Biasi et al., 2020; Mathew et al., 2020; Neidleman et al., 2020; Weiskopf et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes findings from other studies with multiple supporting citations.

claim: T cells may be clonally expanded in moderate, but not severe, COVID-19 disease.
source: These T cells may be clonally expanded in moderate, but not severe, disease (Liao et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this finding with supporting citations.

claim: T cell lymphopenia has been a ubiquitous finding in COVID-19.
source: Whereas T cell lymphopenia has been a ubiquitous finding, the effect of COVID-19 on NK cell numbers is more ambiguous, with cytopenia often limited to the most severe cases (Kuri-Cervantes et al., 2020b; Laing et al., 2020; Wilk et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this finding with supporting citations.

claim: The effect of COVID-19 on NK cell numbers is ambiguous, with cytopenia often limited to the most severe cases.
source: Whereas T cell lymphopenia has been a ubiquitous finding, the effect of COVID-19 on NK cell numbers is more ambiguous, with cytopenia often limited to the most severe cases (Kuri-Cervantes et al., 2020b; Laing et al., 2020; Wilk et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this finding with supporting citations.

claim: CD56dim NK cells were maintained in moderate COVID-19 disease, whereas CD56bright NK cells were depleted in both moderate and severe diseases.
source: However, Wilk et al. reported that CD56dim NK cells—key in the cytotoxic antiviral response—were maintained in moderate disease, whereas the CD56bright NK cells (prone to produce pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IFN-γ) were depleted in both moderate and severe diseases (Wilk et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this finding from another study with a supporting citation.

claim: In influenza, depletion of NK cells has been implicated only in severe disease, with normal or even increased NK cell counts after mild disease or vaccination.
source: In influenza, depletion of NK cells has been implicated only in severe disease, with normal or even increased NK cell counts after mild disease or vaccination (Fox et al., 2012; Jost et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this finding with supporting citations.

claim: Monocytes are key players in the innate immune response to pathogens and have been reported to respond divergently to different types of RNA viruses.
source: Monocytes are key players in the innate immune response to pathogens and have been reported to respond divergently to different types of RNA viruses (de Marcken et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this characteristic of monocytes with a supporting citation.

claim: An enhanced type I interferon response in monocytes of patients with COVID-19 has previously been reported.
source: An enhanced type I interferon response in monocytes of patients with COVID-19 has previously been reported (Schulte-Schrepping et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020), but interestingly CAP-flu did not provoke such a strong antiviral response in the expanded monocyte subset.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this finding from other studies with supporting citations.

claim: Interferon evasion and hijacking of the host's ribosomal translational machinery are hallmarks of active viral replication.
source: Interferon evasion and hijacking of the host's ribosomal translational machinery are hallmarks of active viral replication (Chen et al., 2018; García-Sastre, 2011; Walsh and Mohr, 2011).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes these hallmarks with supporting citations.

claim: Both Influenza and SARS-CoV-2 can infect human monocytes.
source: While both Influenza and SARS-CoV-2 can infect human monocytes (Hoeve et al., 2012; Pontelli et al., 2020; Ren et al., 2021), the clear transcriptomic difference in our population could indicate that monocytes in patients with CAP-flu—but not COVID-19—harbored intracellular viruses.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this capability with supporting citations.

claim: Decreased expression of HLA-DR is a hallmark of sepsis in patients with CAP.
source: Due to our limited sample size, and as decreased expression of HLA-DR is a hallmark of sepsis in patients with CAP, these relatively low levels of HLA-DR in monocytes from patients with viral CAP should be interpreted with caution (Venet et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this characteristic with a supporting citation.

claim: IFITM3 plays an essential role in restricting viral replication in CAP-flu.
source: IFITM3 plays an essential role in restricting viral replication in CAP-flu (Yánez et al., 2020), as mice lacking IFITM3 developed severe pulmonary inflammation when infected with an influenza virus of limited virulence (Everitt et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this role with supporting citations.

claim: Mice lacking IFITM3 developed severe pulmonary inflammation when infected with an influenza virus of limited virulence.
source: IFITM3 plays an essential role in restricting viral replication in CAP-flu (Yánez et al., 2020), as mice lacking IFITM3 developed severe pulmonary inflammation when infected with an influenza virus of limited virulence (Everitt et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this experimental finding with a supporting citation.

claim: The causative organism in CAP is typically only identified in approximately 50% of patients.
source: The causative organism in CAP is typically only identified in approximately 50% of patients (Jain et al., 2015; Welte et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this clinical characteristic with supporting citations.

claim: Up to 30% of laboratory-confirmed pneumonia cases can involve viral and bacterial co-infections (most commonly influenza and S. pneumoniae).
source: We nevertheless decided to include this patient to create a realistic representation of patients with CAP-flu, as up to 30% of laboratory-confirmed pneumonia cases can involve viral and bacterial co-infections (most commonly influenza and S. pneumoniae) (Gupta et al., 2008; Jain et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this clinical characteristic with supporting citations.

claim: The study performed CITE-Seq on peripheral blood mononuclear cells from patients.
source: Here, we performed CITE-Seq—Cellular Indexing of Transcriptomes and Epitopes by Sequencing (Stoeckius et al., 2017)—on peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from age-, sex-, and disease severity-matched patients with CAP caused by either SARS-CoV-2, Influenza A, or other pathogens admitted to a non-intensive care ward.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the methodology used with a supporting citation.

claim: CITE-Seq integrates single-cell RNA-sequencing with highly multiplexed surface protein marker detection, akin to classical flow cytometry.
source: By integrating single-cell RNA-sequencing with highly multiplexed surface protein marker detection—akin to classical flow cytometry—we create a high-resolution snapshot of cellular phenotypes and functional states, offering insight into the peripheral immune features of different etiologies of pneumonia.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the capabilities of the CITE-Seq technique.

claim: The study was part of the ELDER-BIOME project approved by the medical ethical committee of the Amsterdam UMC—location AMC.
source: This study was part of the ELDER-BIOME project (clinicaltrials.gov identifier NCT02928367) approved by the medical ethical committee of the Amsterdam UMC—location AMC.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: Written informed consent was obtained from all participants or their legal representatives.
source: Written informed consent was obtained from all participants or their legal representatives.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the consent process.

claim: All COVID-19 patients had reverse transcription (RT-PCR)-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection, in combination with a CORADS CT-score of 5.
source: All COVID-19 patients had reverse transcription (RT-PCR)-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection, in combination with a CORADS CT-score of 5 (De Smet et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the diagnostic criteria for COVID-19 patients with a supporting citation.

claim: Cell viability was assessed by FACS analysis and was >90% in all samples.
